sections.heading: Receiving the Savior you have given me
sections.text: God of all grace, you have given me a Savior. Please give me faith that does more than agree with the truth — faith that lives from him every day. Make Jesus my deepest desire, my sure hope, and the only glory I want to boast in.
theological_themes: God’s grace in giving Christ as Savior
Christ as the believer’s hope and boast

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that salvation is God’s gift received through faith, not something earned. That grounds the prayer’s opening appeal to the God of grace for faith that rests in the Savior he has given.
Paul describes the Christian life as lived by faith in the Son of God. This supports the request for a faith that not only begins with Christ but continues to live by him.

sections.heading: Learning to depend on Christ in every way
sections.text: Let me run to Jesus as my refuge, build my life on him as my foundation, and walk with him as the road beneath my feet. Let me follow him as my guide, become like him as my example, listen to him as my prophet, depend on his prayers for me as my great high priest, and gladly obey him as my King.
theological_themes: Christ as refuge, foundation, way, and guide
Christ’s threefold office as prophet, priest, and king
discipleship as obedience and conformity to Jesus

scripture_references.connection: Jesus identifies himself as the way to the Father, not merely a teacher of the way. This supports the prayer’s desire to walk in Christ and come to God through him.
Paul says there is no foundation for God’s people other than Jesus Christ. The prayer’s image of building on Christ rests directly on this apostolic teaching.
Hebrews presents Jesus as the great high priest through whom believers draw near for mercy and help. That gives biblical substance to relying on Christ’s intercession rather than on self-confidence.

sections.heading: Staying loyal to Jesus when it costs me
sections.text: Keep me from being embarrassed by Jesus or by what he has said. If following him brings rejection, help me carry that reproach with joy. But do not let me confuse the consequences of my own sin or foolishness with suffering for Christ. Guard my life from careless, unholy choices that would dishonor him. Keep me from taking the crowd as my example, and when your Word calls me forward, do not let me stall or make excuses.
theological_themes: obedience to God’s Word over conformity to the crowd

scripture_references.connection: Jesus warns against being ashamed of him and his words in an unbelieving generation. This directly supports the prayer’s request for open loyalty to Christ and his teaching.
Peter distinguishes suffering unjustly for conscience before God from being punished for wrongdoing. This helps preserve the prayer’s nuance: not all hardship is persecution for Christ.
Paul calls believers not to be conformed to the present age but transformed by God’s renewing work. That undergirds the plea not to make the multitude the model.

sections.heading: Being kept from the pull of this world
sections.text: May your dear Son keep me from this present evil age. When the world smiles, do not let it charm me away from you. When it threatens, do not let fear rule me. When it offers its sins, do not let them stain me. When it teaches lies, do not let them mislead me.
theological_themes: resistance to temptation, fear, corruption, and deception

scripture_references.connection: Paul says Christ gave himself to deliver believers from the present evil age according to the Father’s will. This gives the prayer its frame: preservation from the world is part of Christ’s saving work.
John warns against loving the world’s desires and passing glory. That supports the prayer’s concern that the world’s attractions, pressures, vices, and errors not pull the believer away from God.

sections.heading: Living here as someone headed home
sections.text: Help me feel, deep down, that I am not finally at home here. Make my life plainly say that I am looking for a better country — the home you have promised. Let my confidence in my place there become clearer, my character more fitted for it, and my taste of its joy more real and frequent.
theological_themes: growth in holiness as preparation for glory

scripture_references.connection: Hebrews describes the faithful as strangers and exiles who desire a better, heavenly country. This is the clearest biblical foundation for the prayer’s pilgrim language and longing for home with God.

Paul locates the believer’s citizenship in heaven and connects it with the future transformation Christ will bring. That supports both the present identity of the Christian and the hope toward which the prayer looks.

sections.heading: Doing everything in Jesus’ name
sections.text: And in whatever I do — ordinary or important, seen or unseen — let it be done in the name of my Savior, with trust in him, obedience to him, and thanks to you through him. Amen.
theological_themes: the whole life lived under Christ’s name

scripture_references.connection: Paul commands believers to do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to the Father through him. This directly grounds the prayer’s closing desire that the whole of life be offered through Christ.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original phrase about the believer’s “title” to the heavenly country becoming clearer could be misunderstood as a legal right to heaven that grows by sanctification. I rendered it as growing confidence in one’s place there, while treating fitness for heaven as growth in holiness rather than the basis of acceptance with God.

The language of being preserved from “this present evil world” can sound like rejection of creation or ordinary human culture. I interpreted it in the biblical sense of the fallen world-system opposed to God, not the physical world God made good.
The prayer carefully distinguishes reproach for Christ from suffering consequences for one’s own wrongdoing. That distinction is biblically important and was preserved explicitly.
significant_interpretive_choices: I unfolded the compact Puritan sequence of Christ as refuge, foundation, way, guide, example, prophet, priest, and king into contemporary relational language while keeping each image present.
I rendered “never delay when thy Word invites me to advance” as prompt obedience when God’s Word calls me forward, rather than as a general call to ambition or activism.
I treated “foretastes” of the heavenly country as present experiences of the joy and hope of the coming inheritance, without implying that present feelings are the ground of assurance.
